result:
Both integrate changes from one branch into another; they differ in what they do to history.

**Merge** ties the two histories together with a new merge commit. Existing commits are untouched.

```
before:            after `git merge main` (on feature):
A---B---C main     A---B---C-------M feature
     \                  \         /
      D---E feature      D-------E
```

**Rebase** replays your commits on top of the other branch, creating new commits with new hashes. History becomes a straight line.

```
before:            after `git rebase main` (on feature):
A---B---C main     A---B---C main
     \                      \
      D---E feature          D'---E' feature
```

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserved as it happened, with branches | Rewritten into a linear sequence |
| Commit hashes | Unchanged | Changed for the replayed commits |
| Conflicts | Resolved once, in the merge commit | Resolved commit by commit as each is replayed |
| Safe on shared branches | Yes | No, because it rewrites commits others may have |
| Undo | Revert or reset the merge commit | Recover the old tip via `git reflog` |

**Rule of thumb:**
- Rebase your own local, unpushed work to tidy it up or to catch up with `main`.
- Merge when integrating into a shared branch, or when the branch has already been pushed and others are using it.

Don't rebase commits other people have based work on: their history will diverge from yours, and you'll need a force push (`git push --force-with-lease`) to publish the rewritten branch.
